title: Interfaces & Object Shapes
description: Model data structures with interfaces — the backbone of typed configs, API responses, and domain objects.

challenges.title: What is an interface?
challenges.description:
What does a TypeScript interface define?

  A)  A class that can be instantiated
  B)  The shape of an object — what properties and types it must have
  C)  A runtime value that validates objects
  D)  A function signature only
challenges.whyMatters: Every config object, API response, and domain model you work with has a shape — interfaces let you express that shape and catch mismatches at compile time.
hints: Interfaces describe structure, not implementation — they exist only at compile time

choices.label: A)  A class that can be instantiated
B)  The shape of an object — what properties and types it must have
C)  A runtime value that validates objects

challenges.title: Define a User interface
challenges.description:
Define a `User` interface with three required fields:
- `id` (string)
- `name` (string)
- `email` (string)

Then write a function `createUser(id, name, email)` that returns a `User`.
challenges.whyMatters: Defining and using typed user objects is one of the first things you do in any application — auth systems, dashboards, APIs.
hints: Declare each field inside the interface body with its type — all three are primitive string types
The return type of createUser should be: User

challenges.title: Function accepting an interface
challenges.description:
Define an `AppConfig` interface with:
- `name` (string)
- `version` (string)
- `port` (number)

Then write a function `formatConfig(config: AppConfig): string` that returns a string in this format:
`"name v1.0 on port 8080"`
challenges.whyMatters: Functions that accept typed objects are the core of any typed API — you describe the shape once and every caller gets checked against it.
hints: Build the return string by embedding the three config fields — note the fixed text fragments (v, on port) that appear between them
The parameter type is: config: AppConfig

challenges.title: Optional properties
challenges.description:
Write an interface `ServiceConfig` with:
- `host` (string, required)
- `port` (number, required)
- `timeout` (number, optional)
- `retries` (number, optional)

Then write `buildUrl(config: ServiceConfig): string` that returns `"http://localhost:8080"`.
challenges.whyMatters: Optional config fields are everywhere — timeouts, retry counts, feature flags. TypeScript makes it explicit which fields can be absent.
hints: Use ? for optional properties: timeout?: number
Combine the fixed protocol prefix, host, and port with the correct separators in a template literal

challenges.title: Readonly properties
challenges.description:
Write an interface `DbConfig` with three `readonly` properties:
- `host` (string)
- `port` (number)
- `dbName` (string)

Then write `createDbConfig(host, port, dbName): DbConfig` that returns a new DbConfig.
challenges.whyMatters: Readonly config objects prevent accidental mutation — critical when the same config object is shared across multiple services.
hints: Add readonly before each property: readonly host: string
The return type is DbConfig — TypeScript enforces readonly at the call site

challenges.title: Extending interfaces
challenges.description:
Model a deployment manifest using two interfaces:

`Resource` with: `id` (string), `name` (string), `labels` (Record<string, string>)

`Deployment` extending `Resource` with: `image` (string), `replicas` (number), `env` (Record<string, string>, optional)

Write `describeDeployment(d: Deployment): string` returning:
`[id] name → image x replicas replicas`
challenges.whyMatters: Extending interfaces models inheritance in your domain — a DeployedService extends Service extends Resource. Common in infrastructure typings.
hints: Use extends: interface Deployment extends Resource { ... }
Follow the output format from the description exactly — embed each field at the right position, with the surrounding punctuation as literal text

challenges.title: Index signatures
challenges.description:
Write an interface `LabelMap` with an index signature: any string key maps to a string value.

Then write `mergeLabels(a: LabelMap, b: LabelMap): LabelMap` that merges two label maps — if both have the same key, `b` wins.
challenges.whyMatters: Dynamic key-value maps appear in Kubernetes labels, HTTP headers, and environment configs — index signatures are how you type them.
hints: The spread operator (...) lets you combine two objects into one — check the concept card for how it works

challenges.title: Method signatures
challenges.description:
Write a `Counter` interface with four method signatures:
- `increment(): void`
- `decrement(): void`
- `value(): number`
- `reset(): void`

Then write `createCounter(initial?: number): Counter` that returns an object implementing the interface.
challenges.whyMatters: Interfaces with method signatures are how you type factories, plugins, and service objects — the caller knows the contract without seeing the implementation.
hints: Declare a mutable variable inside createCounter before the return statement — initialize from the optional parameter, falling back to 0 if absent
Return an object literal with all four methods

challenges.title: Bring it together
challenges.description:
Define two nested interfaces:

`Address`: `street` (string), `city` (string), `country` (string), `postCode` (string, optional)

`Contact`: `id` (string), `firstName` (string), `lastName` (string), `email` (string), `phone` (string, optional), `address` (Address)

Then write two functions that each return a formatted string:
- `fullName(contact: Contact): string` — returns the contact's full name, e.g. Alice Smith
- `formatContact(contact: Contact): string` — returns a single-line summary, e.g. Alice Smith <alice@example.com> - London
challenges.whyMatters: Nested interfaces with optional properties mirror real-world data — every CRM, HR system, and user API you'll ever work with has a shape like this.
hints: Both functions return a plain string — build it with a template literal using the contact fields
formatContact needs the full name, email, and city — you already have a function that gives you the full name
